meta.method: deterministic rule-based analysis, rules documented in docs/ADVISOR_METHODOLOGY.md

R3.spec_basis: illustrative pipeline quality values, dry basis, not a contract spec

meta.note: findings are recomputed from the model on every rebuild; with a different design they change, including to no action justified. All numbers are synthetic and educational. The pipeline specification is illustrative only.

findings.title: Hydrogen supply to the methanation step
findings.problem: Checks whether the methanation step runs short of hydrogen. The model flags this itself (h2_limited). The check fires when the flag is set and achieved CO2 conversion falls over 5 points short.

evidence.summary: The catalyst can convert 90.0 percent of the CO2. The gas only lets it reach 8.5 percent. Hydrogen runs out first: 0.00 kmol/h of H2 leaves the reactor. CO2 left in the dry product: 7.94 mol percent.
details: Requested CO conversion 98.0 percent; achieved 98.0 percent.
Requested CO2 conversion 90.0 percent; achieved 8.5 percent. Shortfall 81.5 points (fires above 5; high severity above 30).
Hydrogen leaving the reactor: 0.00 kmol/h. Near-zero slip (under 0.5 mol percent) confirms the shortage.
Cause in the model: the shift step targets H2/CO = 3. That ratio feeds the CO reaction only. It leaves no hydrogen for the CO2 reaction.

possible_causes.cause: The shift extent target covers CO methanation only. This is read straight from the model settings and flows.
In a real plant, shift catalyst decay or bypassing could add to the shortfall.

findings.recommendation: Retarget the shift extent to full methanation stoichiometry (the model's wgs_target "stoichiometric" mode). It makes exactly enough hydrogen for both methanation reactions. Review the trade-offs below before adopting it.

expected_impact.summary: The retargeted design was run in the same model, same feed. CO2 in the dry product falls from 7.94 to 0.99 mol percent. Achieved CO2 conversion rises from 8.5 to 90.0 percent. SNG production falls by 445.7 kg/h. Steam use rises by 251.8 kg/h.

calculations.label: CO2 in dry product, after retarget
H2 in dry product after retarget

assumptions: Both designs run at the same feed rate and the same catalyst conversions.
Annual figures assume 8,000 operating hours per year.
The CO2 removal step keeps its design removal fraction in the base comparison.

sensitivity.description: Production loss from the retarget, computed at CO2 removal of 85, 90, 95 percent. Each point compares the two designs at the same removal.

findings.tradeoffs: The fix costs product. SNG output falls by 445.7 kg/h (16.2 percent). Steam demand rises by 251.8 kg/h (36.5 percent). Unreacted hydrogen (6.4 mol percent dry) leaves in the product. Shift reactor cooling rises by 152.4 kW.

quality_gate.check: CO in the dry product must stay within 0.1 mol percent after the change.
quality_gate.note: Computed CO after the change: 0.81 mol percent dry (was 0.98). It improves but stays above the 0.1 limit. Closing that gap needs the separate measures in R3 and R4.

validation_required: A shift reactor check that the larger extent is feasible at the catalyst's conditions.
A steam supply check for the higher make-up rate.

findings.title: Heat integration: reactor heat against feed preheat
findings.problem: The methanation reactor gives off a lot of heat. The feed needs heating before the shift reactor. This check compares the two duties from the energy block. It fires when recoverable reactor heat (60 to 85 percent assumed) exceeds the preheat duty at the base estimate.

evidence.summary: Reactor cooling duty is 3,847.2 kW. Feed preheat duty is 940.2 kW. Even the low recovery estimate (2,308.3 kW) covers the preheat.
details: Methanation reactor cooling duty: 3,847.2 kW.
Feed preheat duty (40 to 300 C): 940.2 kW.
Recoverable heat: 2,308.3 kW at 60 percent, 2,789.2 kW at 72.5 percent, 3,270.1 kW at 85 percent.

possible_causes.cause: The design heats the feed with outside utility. At the same time it rejects far more reactor heat to cooling. Both duties are computed in the energy block.

findings.recommendation: Add a feed-effluent heat exchanger (gas-gas interchanger). Let the hot reactor outlet heat the incoming feed. This removes the external preheat duty.

expected_impact.summary: The exchanger removes the whole preheat duty: 940.2 kW. That is 7,521,600 kWh per year at 8,000 hours. Reactor cooling still needed after recovery: 2,907.0 kW.
assumptions: Between 60 and 85 percent of the reactor heat is recoverable at useful temperature.
The plant runs 8,000 hours per year.
The exchanger can be sized to deliver the full preheat duty.

sensitivity.description: Saving equals the smaller of recoverable heat and the preheat duty. All three recovery estimates exceed the preheat duty here. So the saving is capped at the preheat duty in every case.

findings.tradeoffs: An exchanger adds capital cost and pressure drop. Start-up needs a separate heater until the reactor is hot.

quality_gate.check: Product quality must not change. Heat exchange moves heat only, not mass.
quality_gate.note: In this model the product composition is unchanged by the exchanger. A real design must still hold the reactor inlet temperature. Confirm product purity during commissioning.

validation_required: Exchanger sizing with real approach temperatures (not in this model).
A start-up heater sized for cold starts.

findings.title: Product gas against pipeline quality
findings.problem: Compares the dry product with an illustrative pipeline specification. The spec is CH4 above 95, CO below 0.1, inert gas (CO2 plus N2) below 4 mol percent. These are illustrative values, not a contract spec. The check fires when any component is out.

evidence.summary: The dry product misses 3 of 3 illustrative limits. CH4 79.0 (wants above 95), CO 0.98 (limit 0.1), inert gas 20.0 (limit 4) mol percent.
details: CH4 is 79.0 mol percent against above 95. Gap: 16.0 points. Closing it means removing inert gas and slip, see the items below.
CO is 0.98 mol percent against below 0.1. Gap: 0.88 points. Candidates: hydrogen recycle, a polishing methanation stage, or a membrane. Each is a hypothesis to evaluate, not a sized design.

Inert gas is 20.0 mol percent against below 4. N2 alone is 12.1 points and CO2 is 7.9 points. Deeper CO2 removal addresses the CO2 share. N2 must be managed at the gasifier, for example oxygen or indirect gasification. Both are hypotheses to evaluate, not sized designs.
Evidence from the CO2 removal sweep: deeper removal helps but cannot close the CH4 gap alone. At 95 percent removal the purity reaches 82.6 percent CH4.

possible_causes.cause: N2 enters at 4.0 mol percent of the feed. It passes through untouched and concentrates to 12.1 in the dry product.
CO2 slips past the removal step and past the hydrogen-starved methanation (see R1).
CO slips through at the design conversion (98.0 percent), see R4.

findings.recommendation: Evaluate three design additions as studies, not sized equipment. One: deeper CO2 removal, to cut the CO2 share of the inerts. Two: hydrogen recycle or a membrane, to cut CO and H2 slip. Three: nitrogen management at the gasifier, such as oxygen or indirect gasification. Each needs its own balance, cost and quality case before adoption.
findings.tradeoffs: Each addition adds cost and complexity. Deeper CO2 removal also cuts the product mass flow.
validation_required: A gasification study for low-nitrogen syngas (oxygen or indirect gasification).
A CO2 removal depth study with product purity and energy balanced.
A CO and H2 slip study (recycle, polishing stage or membrane).

findings.title: CO slip risk as the catalyst ages
findings.problem: Finds the lowest CO conversion that keeps product CO within 0.1 mol percent. Uses the conversion sweep, plus a direct model solve when the sweep never passes. A safe design sits at least 1.0 points above that minimum.

evidence.summary: No sweep point keeps CO within 0.1 mol percent. The model solve needs 99.80 percent conversion. The design runs at 98.0 percent and gives 0.98 CO.
details: Sweep range: CO in product falls from 7.32 at 85.0 to 0.24 at 99.5 percent conversion.
Minimum conversion for the 0.1 limit: 99.80 percent (from a direct model solve by bisection).
The design runs at 98.0 percent conversion. Its product holds 0.98 mol percent CO.
Aged catalyst evidence: at 90.0 percent conversion the product holds 4.88 mol percent CO.
Values are mol percent of the product gas, which holds about half a percent water.

possible_causes.cause: Unconverted CO passes straight to the product. Nothing downstream removes it.
In a real plant, ageing, poisoning or channelling would pull conversion down further.

findings.recommendation: Fit a product CO analyser with an alarm at 0.1 mol percent. Treat CO conversion below 99.80 percent as out of spec for this limit. The design at 98.0 percent cannot hold that with a 1.0 point margin. So pair monitoring with a design addition from R3, such as hydrogen recycle.
validation_required: Catalyst vendor data for end-of-run conversion (not in the model).
A product gas analyser specification and calibration plan.

findings.title: What this model leaves out
findings.problem: Lists what the model leaves out and what a real design step would add. Nothing is invented to fill these gaps.

evidence.summary: Four model gaps limit the findings above. One gap is quantified: the condenser duty misses the latent heat of the water.
details: Kinetics and reactor sizing: conversions are inputs, not computed. A real step solves rate equations and equilibrium at 350 C. Then it sizes the catalyst bed.
Recycle: there is no product gas recycle. Real SNG plants recycle gas to control the temperature rise. Recycle changes conversion per pass and the cooling split.

Condenser duty: only sensible heat is counted. The condensed water (1,326.5 kg/h) also releases latent heat. At about 2,400 kJ/kg that is roughly 884 kW more cooling. The reported condenser duty (626.8 kW) is therefore understated.
Costs: no capital or operating costs are modelled. A real step adds equipment costing and utility prices. Without costs, the findings rank engineering effort, not money.

findings.recommendation: Treat every finding as a screening result. Close these gaps before committing to equipment: kinetics, recycle, condenser latent heat and costs.
validation_required: A kinetic reactor model and bed sizing at the 350 C outlet.
A recycle flowsheet study for reactor temperature control.
A condenser rating that includes latent heat (about 884 kW extra here).
Capital and operating cost estimates for every recommendation.
